He tears his eyes away after a moment, and turns towards the seat Amycus pointed out to him. A black-haired man, leaning against the bar and a blond sit there already, murmuring. Akio hesitates, and then goes over.

The occupants of the space pause and look up at him as he approaches, They eye him questioningly, from his paint stained t-shirt to his black cargo pants.

“Um,” he offers to the blank stares. “Amy- Amycus told me to stay here?”

“…are you even old enough to be in here?” asks the blond, ~~incredulous~~.

“…I am!” Akio lies, having learnt from his previous conversation. It doesn’t matter much. The two men clearly don’t believe him and look at each other for a long moment.

“Whatever,” the man ~~says~~ tiredly, swiping a hand down his face. “Sit.”

He sits. “I’m Akio,” he says again, because he was raised a polite young man. Probably. It’s not coming to him very easily right now.

“I’m Luca Brando,” the blond responds, and nudges his silent friend in the side. “This is Leifr Ásjá.”

“Akio is an interesting name,” says Leifr, not even wincing as Luca’s elbow digs harshly into his side. “You’re a Futaba?”

“Er, yes,” he responds, caught off-guard because these people are from the *most influential Families in the Empire. Why am I here.*

“What?” Luca turns seemingly distracted from tormenting his friend’s organs. “The Futaba? You guys are still around?”

This, sadly, is a normal reaction to hearing his family name. When it’s recognized at all. “Yeah, um, we. We’re mostly with the Doctors nowadays?”

Leifr nods along like randomly encountering a member of a dying clan is normal. “I know a relative of yours. Futaba Masamichi?”

Akio pauses. Luca’s elbow starts moving back in for a sneak attack. “Yeah that’s. That’s my brother.”

The man nods and shoves his friend away without even looking. Luca sneers at him and steals his drink. Leifr just reaches over the counter, pulls out a bottle *(is that even allowed?)* and a new glass and pours out a generous splash.

A storm arrives carrying more than just rain.
Dark clouds cover the sky. Thunder rolls far away. Soon, heavy rain starts to fall. It beats hard against the windows and streets.
Lynn sits by the window alone. For many days, she has felt sad and tired. Small troubles and worries make her upset. She stays away from friends and quiets herself down, thinking the dark mood will never leave.
Strong wind shakes the old tree in the street. Its leaves are bent by the storm, but the tree still stands straight. Rain washes off the dirt on every leaf and stone.
Watching the rain, Lynn slowly calms down.
She understands that storms are not only bad.
They clean the dirty air, wash away tiredness, and let everything start fresh.
Slowly, thunder stops. The heavy rain turns into light drizzle. Dark clouds move away, and the sky becomes clear again. Cool wind blows in, bringing the fresh smell of grass and wet earth.
Lynn takes a deep breath.
This storm brought more than rain.
It brought peace and hope. It washed away her sadness and gave her a new start.
After the storm, everything looks bright again.

**Why Human Creativity Still Matters in the Age of AI** Artificial intelligence has made remarkable strides in recent years. From generating realistic images to composing music and writing essays, AI systems can now produce content that once required significant human effort. However, despite these advances, the rise of AI-generated content—sometimes dismissively called "AI slop"—raises important questions about the value of human creativity. First, human creativity is inherently tied to lived experience. When a person writes a story, paints a picture, or composes a song, they draw upon emotions, memories, and perspectives that no algorithm can truly replicate. AI may mimic patterns, but it does not feel joy, sorrow, or nostalgia. It does not know what it means to love, to lose, or to hope. These elements give human art its depth and authenticity. Second, human creativity involves intention and meaning. A writer chooses each word deliberately, considering tone, audience, and purpose. An AI, by contrast, generates text based on statistical probabilities. It does not understand what it is saying. It has no message to convey, no truth to express. The result may look convincing, but it lacks the soul of genuine communication. Third, creativity is a process, not just a product. The struggle to find the right word, the the right phrase, the moment of breakthrough after hours of frustration—these experiences shape the creator and give the final work its meaning. AI bypasses this entirely. It offers a shortcut, but shortcuts often lead to shallow destinations. Moreover, human creativity fosters connection. When we read a poem or hear a story, we connect with another person's inner world. We recognize shared feelings, struggles, and triumphs. AI-generated content may entertain, but it rarely moves us in the same way. We know, deep down, that no one was truly behind the words. And that matters. The number glowed faintly under the moonlight—an old, faded jersey stretched across a broad silhouette. James barely made out the white numerals before his heart dropped into his stomach.

Eleven.

That number had haunted him for years. The same number his bully had worn during every practice, every game, every hallway shove. He could still hear the laughter, the taunts, the name-calling that followed him home each day. And now—after all these years—that jersey was closing in on him.

He grabbed his friend's wrist and ducked behind a rusted dumpster. "Don't move. Don't breathe."

The footsteps grew louder. Closer. A shadow passed the alley entrance, stopped, and turned slowly. James pressed himself against the cold brick, his friend's hand gripping his in the dark.

Ten seconds. Twenty. Then the footsteps continued, fading into the distance.

They stayed still for two more minutes before James finally exhaled.

"I thought I left this town behind for good," he whispered.

His friend looked at him—eyes searching, not quite understanding. "Who was that?"

James couldn't answer. Not yet. Instead, he nodded toward the old path that led up the hill. "We need to keep moving. The hangout isn't far."

They ran in silence, weaving through back alleys and overgrown shortcuts that James remembered from childhood. His lungs burned. The night air was cold against his sweat-soaked skin. Every shadow seemed alive, every creak a signal that he'd been found.

Finally, they reached the clearing. The old treehouse. The meeting spot. The one place that had ever felt safe.

James stopped.

The treehouse was gone. Boarded up. Demolished. Nothing remained but a concrete slab and a pile of splintered wood, as if someone had erased his last good memory.

He stood there, staring at the rubble, the air leaving his lungs differently now.

"It's gone..."

His friend stepped beside him, quiet for a long moment. Then, without a word, he placed a hand on James's shoulder—steady, firm, present.
